queue.tree_name: The Moreton Bay Fig of Jardim Constantino
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its wide 26 metre crown and buttressing roots, the shade tree of a quarter-hectare garden. It stands in Jardim Constantino, a few steps from the paperbark.
queue.story:
A garden of a quarter of a hectare in Arroios holds a fig with a 26 metre crown, which accounts for most of the shade in the place. Jardim Constantino is small: a lake, a playground, a statue of Prometheus and two protected trees. This is the wide one.

Ficus macrophylla comes from the east coast of Australia and was planted across Lisbon in the late 19th and early 20th centuries for exactly this reason. It grows fast, throws a dense crown, and drops the buttressing roots that make a mature specimen look like it is holding the ground down. At 24 metres tall on a trunk 2.33 metres round, this one has done the job.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its white, spongy bark peeling in papery sheets on a tall, thin 18 metre tree. It stands in Jardim Constantino, a few steps from the garden's wide Moreton Bay fig.
queue.story:
Lisbon has one prickly paperbark, and this is it. The Portuguese record of Jardim Constantino calls the tree unique in the city, which is a strong claim for a garden of a quarter of a hectare to hold.

Melaleuca styphelioides is an Australian tree grown for its bark: white, spongy, laid down in papery layers you can press a thumb into, peeling in sheets around a trunk 1.58 metres round. The leaves are small, stiff and sharp-tipped, which is the prickly half of the name. At 18 metres with an 11 metre crown it is the tall thin one in this garden. The fig a few steps away is the wide one.

queue.tree_name: The Weeping Fig of Campo Santana
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the glossy leaves and the fine roots hanging from its limbs. It stands fifty paces from the yew on the same slope, five metres round with its crown twenty metres up.
queue.story: Ficus benjamina is the tree most people know as a pot plant, the glossy thing sulking in an office corner and shedding leaves whenever somebody moves it. Fifty paces from the yew, on the same slope, one of them has a trunk five metres around and a crown twenty metres up. Portugal classified it on exactly the same day as the yew, 21 May 1968, and the national register still files it under a second name that says what the species does when nothing stops it: matapalo, tree killer. Like its Moreton Bay relatives it can begin high in another tree and work downward, and even planted honestly in soil it keeps the habit of letting fine roots down from the limbs. One useful correction before you go.
queue.name: The Weeping Fig of Campo Santana
queue.worth: the tree already has one: ship this only if it is better
